Data-Driven Decision Making in Latent Heterogeneous Environments

Details

Event Description

Abstract: Most learning-and-decision systems assume a single, homogeneous response to actions. In practice—marketing, healthcare, operations—outcomes vary across unobserved segments. This talk develops a data-driven framework for decision making under latent heterogeneity, where each individual belongs to an unknown group and group membership is probabilistic and feature-driven. I will focus on a linear contextual bandit model with a logistic “gating” rule for membership and group-specific linear rewards, and present an exploration-free, phased algorithm that jointly learns the gate and the segment-specific response surfaces via a high-dimensional EM procedure with sparsity control.

On the theory side, I will show finite-sample estimation guarantees and two notions of regret. We prove that “strong regret”—measured against an oracle that knows the realized segment—cannot be sublinear due to inherent misclassification; in contrast, the practically relevant “regular regret”—against an oracle that knows only the parameters—achieves minimax-optimal rates in horizon and dimension. The results clarify when margin conditions help, and why classical logT regret is unattainable once a stochastic gating boundary must be learned.

A case study on a large-scale cash-bonus targeting platform illustrates substantial gains over pooled models and performance close to a segment-aware oracle. I will close with mechanism-design ideas (screening, deposits, deadlines, proper scoring) that can incentivize users to self-identify their realized segment—pointing to a joint algorithmic-economic toolkit for AI decisions in latent heterogeneous environments. 

Stochastic Linear Bandits with Latent Heterogeneity (Paper)
